newsitem.title: USA: Dividend payout fills Alaskans' banks accounts.
newsitem.headline: Dividend payout fills Alaskans' banks accounts.

text.p: Most Alaskans became $1,130 richer on Wednesday as the state's oil trust fund began sending out its annual dividends.
The 15th annual Permanent Fund payout is the largest ever, going to more than 542,000 people, nearly all the 600,000 men, women and children in Alaska.
To qualify for the payment, residents must live in Alaska year-round -- with some exceptions for college students, military personnel and others -- and must have lived in the state for two years.
The record dividend was the result of record earnings for the $17.6 billion fund, set up in 1977 when oil began flowing through the trans-Alaska pipeline.
Most recipients got their payments on Wednesday. For the fourth year, the fund is shipping dividends electronically to recipients' bank accounts.
Sixty-one percent of the recipients requested direct deposit, said Jim Kelly, spokesman for the Alaska Permanent Fund Corp., the state agency that manages the fund's investments.
Those who did not get their dividends deposited directly will receive them in the mailbox, with the mailing to start on Thursday.
Though not an official holiday, dividend day is one of the most eagerly awaited milestones in the Alaska year -- especially for retailers and merchants.
This year's payment pumps $613.3 million into residents' hands, accounting for 5 percent of the average Alaska family's disposable income.

"It's Permanent Fun Time!" and "Permanent Fund Fun!" proclaim travel company advertisements. Others are advertising dividend sales for furniture, cars -- a "Double-Your-Dividend" promotion promises to multiply the dividend amount for a down payment -- snowmachines and even ice-cream treats.
Many Alaskans choose to spend their windfall on vacations.
Alaska Airlines, United, Northwest, Reno Air, America West and Delta all offer multi-ticket packages for the dividend total.

"One of the things people do when they get a fairly large amount of money, a windfall like this, is they want to travel," said Jack Evans, a spokesman for Alaska Airlines. "The opportunity to travel and to see destinations you normally wouldn't be able to see is attractive to a lot of people."
His company unveiled its four-ticket dividend package on Sept. 26, the morning after the Alaska Permanent Fund board announced, on live television, the dividend total.
The other airlines followed suit, continuing a practice started by defunct Anchorage-based MarkAir.
